subject: physics_2
question_text: What is Doppler effect? Obtain an expression for the apparent frequency of sound heard when the source is in motion with respect to an observer at rest?

verification.note: The 1+1+2+2+2 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it — the figure carries 0 marks because the question does not ask for a diagram. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Physics hand-checked: t₁ = L/V; t₂ = T + (L − VₛT)/V; T′ = t₂ − t₁ = T(V − Vₛ)/V; n′ = 1/T′ = n·V/(V − Vₛ) > n for approach, and n′ = n·V/(V + Vₛ) < n for recession. This is the moving-SOURCE derivation — the crest spacing (wavelength) changes; the moving-observer case is a genuinely different derivation and lives on its own card.

recall_prompt: Say the derivation in order — the set-up, the arrival times of the two crests, the apparent period, and the apparent frequency.

steps.label: Doppler effect defined
steps.mark_note: Apparent change due to relative motion
lines: The apparent change in the frequency of
sound due to relative motion between the
source and the observer is known as the
Doppler effect.
steps.margin_note: First mark. State the definition before the derivation — apparent change, relative motion.
steps.why: The derivation below computes exactly what this sentence claims: how motion alone changes the frequency the observer receives while the source emits the same n throughout.
common_mistakes: Dropping the word apparent — the source's own frequency never changes.
Starting the derivation without the definition — the question asks for both.

recall.must_convey: That the Doppler effect is the apparent change in frequency caused by relative motion between source and observer.
accept: relative motion between source and observer
the heard frequency changes, not the emitted one
reject: the first crest takes L by V

steps.memory_tip: One sentence, two key words: apparent and relative.

steps.label: The geometry
steps.margin_note: S emits the first crest; one period later the source stands at S′, a distance VₛT nearer to O.
steps.why: The whole derivation is in this picture: the second crest starts its journey VₛT closer to the observer, so it needs less travel time — the two arrival times differ by less than T.
common_mistakes: Moving the observer in this figure — in this case only the SOURCE moves; O stays fixed.

recall.must_convey: That the source moves from S to S′ (a distance VₛT) between the two crests, while O stays fixed at distance L.
accept: mark S, S dash and O
the source moves V s T toward the observer
reject: T dash is T into V minus V s by V

steps.memory_tip: Three ticks on a line — S, S′, O — and the three distances L, VₛT, L − VₛT between them.

steps.label: Set-up and the first crest
lines: A source S and an observer O at rest are
a distance L apart. The source emits
sound of frequency n and time period T;
V is the speed of sound in air.
The source moves toward O with velocity
Vₛ, and releases the first crest at S.
The crest travels the full distance L:
steps.margin_note: One mark. Name every symbol, then the first arrival time L/V.
steps.why: The first crest leaves before the motion matters — it covers the full original distance L at the speed of sound. It is the reference against which the second crest's earlier arrival will be measured.
common_mistakes: Writing t₁ = L/(V − Vₛ) — the crest travels at the speed of sound V in still air; the source's motion never changes the speed of the sound already emitted.
Leaving symbols undefined — n, T, V, Vₛ and L must each be introduced.

recall.must_convey: That source and observer start a distance L apart and the first crest arrives after t₁ = L/V.
accept: the first crest takes L by V
source moves toward the observer with V s
reject: the second crest travels L minus V s T

steps.memory_tip: Crest one leaves before the source has moved — plain distance over speed, L/V.

steps.label: The second crest
lines: The source releases the second crest one
time period T later. In that time the
source has moved a distance VₛT toward
O and stands at S′, so the second crest
travels only L − VₛT:
steps.margin_note: Two marks: the shortened distance L − VₛT, and the T added for the later start.
steps.why: Both pieces of t₂ matter: the crest starts T later (the emission delay) but travels a shorter path (the motion). The competition between those two is the whole Doppler effect.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the leading T — the second crest is EMITTED at time T, then travels.
Writing L + VₛT — the source approaches, so the remaining distance shrinks.

recall.must_convey: That the second crest leaves T later from a point VₛT closer, so t₂ = T + (L − VₛT)/V.
accept: travels only L minus V s T
t two is T plus L minus V s T over V
reject: the first crest takes L by V

steps.memory_tip: Later start (+T), shorter road (L − VₛT) — write both, in that order.

steps.label: Apparent time period
lines: The observer receives the two crests a
time T′ apart — the apparent time
period:

lines.text: T′ = t₂ − t₁ = T + (L − VₛT)/V − L/V

steps.margin_note: Two marks: subtract the arrival times and watch L cancel — the answer must not contain L.
steps.why: L cancels because the effect does not depend on how far away the source is, only on how fast it approaches — a result that checks itself: any surviving L would mean an algebra slip.
common_mistakes: Keeping L in the final expression — the L/V terms cancel exactly.
Sign slip in the bracket — approach must SHORTEN the period: T′ < T.

recall.must_convey: That subtracting the arrival times cancels L and gives T′ = T(V − Vₛ)/V.
accept: subtract t one from t two
T dash is T into V minus V s over V

steps.memory_tip: If L survives the subtraction, redo it — distance must drop out of a rate effect.

steps.label: Apparent frequency
lines: The apparent frequency is the reciprocal
of the apparent time period:
n′ > n: the heard frequency is higher
when the source approaches.
If the source moves away from O, Vₛ
reverses sign:
steps.margin_note: Two marks: invert T′ to get n′, then state both cases with their inequalities.
steps.why: Inverting the period turns the shorter T′ into a higher n′ — the algebra now says what the train example says. Quoting the receding case shows the formula's sign carries the physics.
common_mistakes: Inverting only part of the expression — n′ = 1/T′ inverts the whole bracket.
Writing the approach case with V + Vₛ — check: approach must give n′ > n, so the denominator must shrink.

recall.must_convey: That n′ = 1/T′ = nV/(V − Vₛ), higher than n for approach, with V + Vₛ for recession.
accept: n V by V minus V s
plus V s when moving away

steps.memory_tip: Approach shrinks the denominator, so the frequency grows — the sign always tells the story.

insider_note: This is the crest-timing derivation — two arrival times, subtract, invert. The observer-moving case looks similar but runs on relative sound speed, and mixing the two structures is where this answer loses marks.
